harrison.pages: Harrison 22e Ch.83 Neoplasms of the Lung (p.614-622); SVC syndrome from Ch.80 Oncologic Emergencies (p.585-586)
clinicalPearls: Histology splits into small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and three non-small-cell types (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large-cell) grouped as NSCLC; these four account for about 90% of epithelial lung cancers and the SCLC/NSCLC distinction drives entirely different natural history and management (p.616).

SCLC and NSCLC behave very differently: SCLC is more strongly tobacco-associated, harbours TP53 and RB1 mutations in roughly 90% of cases, and presents with extensive-stage disease in 60-70% of patients (p.617, p.622).

Adenocarcinoma is now the most common subtype as smoking has declined, and predominates in never-smokers/light smokers, women, and younger adults (<60); squamous and small-cell types remain the most tobacco-linked (p.616).

Within NSCLC, distinguishing squamous from nonsquamous is critical for therapy; 'non-small-cell carcinoma, not otherwise specified' is no longer an acceptable diagnosis, and immunohistochemistry (TTF-1/napsin-A for adeno, p40/p63 for squamous) resolves ambiguous small biopsies (p.616).

About two-thirds of new US lung cancer diagnoses occur in former smokers or never-smokers; roughly one in five women and one in 12 men with lung cancer have never smoked, so a never-smoking history does not exclude the diagnosis (p.614).

Smoking cessation benefits patients even after a lung cancer diagnosis (better overall survival, fewer treatment side effects, improved quality of life), yet about 30% continue to smoke after diagnosis (p.614-615).

A normal chest x-ray does not exclude lung cancer: chronic cough with or without haemoptysis in a current/former smoker with COPD aged 40 or older warrants thorough investigation even with a normal CXR (p.618).
Tissue sampling is mandatory to confirm diagnosis in all suspected cases; a core biopsy is preferred over FNA to provide enough material for molecular and PD-L1 testing (p.620).
Central lesions (squamous, small-cell, endobronchial carcinoids) are best reached by bronchoscopy, whereas peripheral lesions (adenocarcinoma, large-cell) favour transthoracic biopsy (p.620).

PET should never be used alone to diagnose lung cancer or confirm mediastinal/metastatic involvement; tissue confirmation is always required, and false positives occur with infection and granulomatous disease such as tuberculosis (p.620).
harrison.pathophysiology: Lung cancer arises from respiratory epithelium (bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli). Environmental carcinogens, chiefly tobacco smoke, drive transformation of bronchoepithelial cells, modulated by polymorphisms in carcinogen-metabolising genes (e.g. CYP1A1). Cancers accumulate gain-of-function oncogene mutations and loss-of-function tumour-suppressor mutations; allelic loss on chromosome 3p occurs very early, even in histologically normal smoke-damaged epithelium. NSCLC adenocarcinomas are frequently driven by targetable oncogenic alterations (EGFR ~10-35%, KRAS ~15-25%, ALK rearrangement 3-7%, plus BRAF, HER2, MET, RET, ROS1, NTRK), whereas nearly 90% of SCLCs carry TP53 and RB1 mutations. Clinical manifestations stem from the primary lesion, local/regional invasion, distant metastases, or paraneoplastic syndromes. Paraneoplastic endocrine effects reflect ectopic hormone secretion: PTH-related peptide (squamous cell) causing hypercalcaemia, ADH or atrial natriuretic peptide (SCLC) causing hyponatraemia, and ectopic ACTH (SCLC, pulmonary carcinoids) causing Cushing-type biochemistry. (p.615-619)
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary metastases from non-lung primaries and other neoplasms metastatic to the lung, which constitutional symptoms cannot reliably distinguish from primary lung cancer (p.619)
Endobronchial metastases from carcinoid, breast, colon, kidney and other tumours presenting with haemoptysis (referenced p.591/Ch.80)
Mesothelioma, which can be hard to separate from adenocarcinoma and is identified by CK5/6, calretinin and WT-1 positivity (p.616)
Pulmonary carcinoid tumour, a neuroendocrine tumour that can also secrete ectopic ACTH (p.619, p.662 area)
infectionMimics: Post-obstructive pneumonia or a persistent pneumonia that does not resolve after repeated antibiotic courses can mask an underlying obstructing tumour (p.618)
Lung abscess physiology from tumour cavitation can mimic infective abscess (p.618)
Granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis can cause false-positive PET uptake and simulate malignancy on imaging (p.620)
nonInfectiousMimics: Paraneoplastic syndromes can mimic metastatic disease and, if unrecognised, lead to inappropriate palliative rather than curative treatment (p.619)

Benign causes of SVC obstruction (central venous catheters, pacemaker/defibrillator leads, aortic aneurysm, thyromegaly, thrombosis, fibrosing mediastinitis from prior radiation/histoplasmosis/Behcet) now account for at least 40% of SVC syndrome cases (p.585)
Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy with periostitis can produce bone pain and a positive bone scan that mimics skeletal metastasis (p.619)
additionalInvestigations: Core biopsy (preferred over FNA) for adequate tissue, obtained by bronchoscopic/transbronchial biopsy, image-guided percutaneous biopsy, or EBUS/EUS-guided sampling depending on location (p.620)

Next-generation sequencing for driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, MET, RET, NTRK, HER2) plus PD-L1 immunohistochemistry reported as tumour proportion score, recommended for all advanced NSCLC (p.620)
Circulating tumour DNA 'liquid biopsy' as a non-invasive adjunct when tissue is limited or inaccessible (p.620)
PET-CT for anatomic staging; an SUV >2.5 is highly suspicious for malignancy, with false negatives in lesions <8 mm, diabetes, and slow-growing tumours (p.620)
MRI of the brain for metastases (and to assess brachial plexus in superior sulcus tumours); recommended in SCLC staging where brain metastases are present in ~10% of asymptomatic patients (p.620-621)
EBUS/EUS-guided or invasive mediastinal staging (mediastinoscopy, thoracoscopy) since one-quarter to one-half of NSCLC patients have mediastinal nodal metastases at diagnosis (p.620-621)
Repeat thoracentesis if the first is negative in suspected malignant pleural effusion; spinal MRI/CT and lumbar puncture if cord compression or leptomeningeal disease is suspected (p.620-621)

Immunohistochemistry panel to confirm neuroendocrine differentiation (CD56/NCAM, synaptophysin, chromogranin, INSM1) and to distinguish primary lung from metastatic adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, napsin-A) (p.616)
Routine labs suggesting metastatic spread: anaemia, and elevated alkaline phosphatase, GGT, transaminases, and calcium (p.619)
redFlags: Chronic cough with or without haemoptysis in a smoker/former smoker with COPD aged 40+, even with a normal chest x-ray (p.618)
A persistent pneumonia without constitutional symptoms that fails to clear after repeated antibiotic courses (p.618)

Superior vena cava syndrome: neck/facial swelling, dilated neck and chest-wall collateral veins, plethora worse when supine; cerebral or laryngeal oedema signals a poorer prognosis and demands urgent evaluation (p.585-586)
Tracheal obstruction from a superior mediastinal mass is the one immediately life-threatening complication and needs emergent therapy (p.586)
Pancoast/superior sulcus tumour: shoulder pain radiating in the ulnar distribution of the arm with destruction of the first and second ribs (p.619)
Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, enophthalmos) from sympathetic chain involvement, often coexisting with Pancoast syndrome (p.619)
Spinal cord compression symptoms (pain, weakness, paralysis, urinary retention) requiring urgent spinal imaging (p.621)

Symptomatic hypercalcaemia (nausea, vomiting, constipation, polyuria, thirst, altered mental status) as the most common life-threatening metabolic complication, usually from squamous cell carcinoma (p.619)
Weight loss exceeding 10% of body weight, a poor prognostic sign (p.619)
harrison.prognosis: Outcome is closely tied to stage at diagnosis, but over half of patients present with locally advanced or metastatic disease. In NSCLC, about 15% have localised disease amenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy, roughly a quarter have local/regional disease that may or may not be curable, and about half have metastatic disease at diagnosis. SEER data (2022) show a 5-year survival of about 63% for localised disease. Extrathoracic metastases are found at autopsy in >50% of squamous, ~80% of adenocarcinoma/large-cell, and >95% of SCLC cases. SCLC is highly likely to present extensive-stage (60-70%). Adenocarcinoma pattern carries prognostic weight: lepidic-predominant is favourable, acinar/papillary intermediate, and solid or micropapillary poor; adenocarcinoma in situ and minimally invasive adenocarcinoma achieve essentially 100% 5-year disease-free survival after complete resection. Weight loss >10%, and thrombotic disease complicating cancer, are poor prognostic signs. (p.616, p.619, p.621-622)
pitfalls: Treating a non-resolving pneumonia with further antibiotics rather than investigating risks losing the chance at early cancer diagnosis (analogous principle stated for head/neck cancer p.611; applied to lung p.618).

Mistaking a paraneoplastic syndrome for metastatic disease and switching to palliative care when the patient may still be curable; many paraneoplastic syndromes resolve with successful tumour treatment (p.619).
Relying on PET alone for diagnosis or staging without tissue confirmation, given false positives from infection/granulomatous disease and false negatives in small or indolent lesions (p.620).
Accepting a negative TTF-1 as excluding a lung primary; a negative TTF-1 does not rule out lung cancer (p.616).
Stopping at a single negative thoracentesis in suspected malignant effusion, or a single negative lumbar puncture in suspected leptomeningeal disease, when a repeat is warranted (p.620-621).

Overly rapid correction of SIADH-related hyponatraemia (including with tolvaptan) can cause irreversible neurologic injury; patients with ectopic ANP may worsen unless sodium intake is increased (p.619).

In screening, ignoring lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis can overstate apparent survival benefit; LDCT also carries a very high false-positive rate (about 96% of positive screens were false positives in NLST) (p.617-618).
harrison.severityClassification: NSCLC: TNM (8th edition, effective 2018; 9th edition expected 2024). T by size/invasion - T1 <=3cm (T1a <=1, T1b >1-2, T1c >2-3), T2 >3-5cm or visceral pleura/main bronchus/atelectasis (T2a >3-4, T2b >4-5), T3 >5-7cm or chest wall/pericardium/phrenic nerve invasion or same-lobe satellite nodule, T4 >7cm or invasion of mediastinum/heart/great vessels/trachea/oesophagus/spine/carina or different ipsilateral-lobe nodule. N: N0 none, N1 ipsilateral peribronchial/hilar/intrapulmonary, N2 ipsilateral mediastinal/subcarinal, N3 contralateral mediastinal/hilar or any scalene/supraclavicular. M: M1a contralateral-lobe nodule or pleural/pericardial nodule/malignant effusion, M1b single distant metastasis to one organ, M1c multiple metastases. SCLC: dual classification recommended - the Veterans Administration two-stage system (limited-stage = confined to ipsilateral hemithorax within a tolerable radiation port, including contralateral supraclavicular nodes, recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement and SVC obstruction; extensive-stage = overt metastatic disease, or cardiac tamponade/malignant effusion/bilateral parenchymal involvement) plus the TNM system, with TNM preferred for the rare apparent stage I SCLC. (p.620-622)

flowcharts.title: Diagnosis and management of lung cancer

nodes.text: Cough, haemoptysis, weight loss or an abnormal chest image
Chest CT with or without PET-CT
Core biopsy by bronchoscopy, EBUS or percutaneous route
IHC, NGS and PD-L1; PET-CT, EBUS and brain MRI staging
Resection, or stereotactic radiation if high surgical risk
Matched targeted therapy, e.g. osimertinib for EGFR
